title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired evaluation comparing a one‑shot NL→config pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation. The preregistered corpus contained 1,200 intent→config tasks (split into two simulated topology clusters), and the preregistration froze a confirmatory paired binary success metric (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). We completed 1,199 paired observations. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Repair was invoked only three times and model_calls_used = 1,203. The preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory per‑cluster test; the archived confirmatory analysis is pooled (see analysis artifacts). Under the supplied task corpus and validator configuration, we find no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline; archived artifacts and provider/validator traces support interpretation and reproducibility.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and systems work emphasize that operational reliability depends on the orchestration stack—model, deterministic verifier, provenance, and sandboxed execution—rather than on the base LLM alone. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated verifier checks constraints, and an iterative repair loop attempts fixes. However, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) versus one‑shot generation remains limited.

We designed NetOpsTraceBench to address this gap with a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study that measures a binary, rollback‑aware episode success on intent→config tasks. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Contributions: (1) a preregistered experimental design and complete execution artifacts (study_id = rX4f7-1); (2) a pooled paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; (3) transparent reporting of execution accounting (repairs invoked, provider audit) and of an analytic deviation to ensure reproducible interpretation.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent system papers frame LLMs as components within broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and call for workflow‑centered evaluation (trace quality, validator interactions, rollback‑aware metrics) rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests. Prior demonstrations show generator+verifier loops in adjacent domains (specification generation, topology compilation) and prototype NetOps tools that combine LLM generation with deterministic parsers or rule checkers. These works document LLM failure modes—hallucination, semantic/unit errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection—that motivate external verification and guarded architectures. However, many demonstrations use constructed corpora and domain‑specific validators, limiting generality; the literature thus motivates preregistered, artifact‑rich paired benchmarks that record provider traces, validator diagnostics, and emulator outcomes for reproducible inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan: The study was preregistered (rX4f7-1) and froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and power assumptions (MDE = 5 pp under assumed baseline≈0.70). The benchmark scope defined 1,200 tasks deterministically generated and split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Implementation: adapter orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1; requested_model = gpt-5-mini; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (baseline and guarded share the same initial candidate per pair to isolate verifier/repair effects). The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces workflow_policies, canonical parsing, and returns validation_before/validation_after diagnostics and a repair_applied flag. Primary binary success requires validator acceptance (validation_after.valid == true), no emulator availability degradation above tolerance, and no automatic rollback.

Topologies and preregistered H3: The preregistration explicitly included H3 (confirmatory per‑cluster paired breakdown across the two simulated topology clusters). The archived confirmatory analysis executed and archived a pooled paired binary analysis only; a confirmatory per‑cluster H3 test was not executed and therefore is not part of the confirmatory artifact set. The absence of per‑cluster confirmatory outputs is reflected in the archived analysis artifacts (pooled contingency table and results). Key archived artifacts for primary inference are available in the run (examples): analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json. These artifacts document the pooled counts, bootstrap parameters (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000), and provider audit counts used for the primary inference.

Design rationale (shared_initial_candidate): We used a shared_initial_candidate per pair so that baseline and guarded conditions start from the identical model proposal; this isolates the verifier/repair mechanism’s marginal effect and prevents generation variance from confounding paired discordance counts. That design reduces variability but also reduces the opportunities for repair to trigger if initial candidates already satisfy validator rules. Execution artifacts (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200; repair = 3) substantiate that repair was rarely invoked under the chosen corpus and validator strictness.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The pipeline completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199). Provider audit: model_calls_used = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1; stage_counts record shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3. Missingness: failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1.

Primary pooled outcomes: The paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_count = 1,196 (0.9974979149); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (1.0). Paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. Representative per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) show validator traces with validation_after.valid = true for the majority of episodes and repair_applied = false.

Topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3): Although the task corpus was generated with two topology clusters, the preregistered per‑cluster confirmatory test H3 was not executed; the archived confirmatory artifacts present pooled paired inference only. Readers and future analysts can compute per‑cluster contingency tables from the archived per‑task scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and rerun per‑cluster analyses if needed; the primary published confirmatory inference in this manuscript is the pooled result described above.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The pooled confirmatory result shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the supplied corpus and validator configuration (p = 0.25; CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded operational explanations are supported. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) left very limited absolute headroom for improvement; the preregistered MDE targeted a 5 pp increase, so the run was underpowered to detect the observed ≈0.25 pp effect. Second, corpus and verifier design materially affected repair invocation: deterministic task generation produced clear required sequences and the deterministic validator accepted most initial candidates, so repair was rarely called (repair = 3). These points are evidenced by analysis/condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation artifacts, and execution/provider audit logs.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong because seeds, deterministic task generation, deterministic validator rules, and automated exclusion rules were frozen. Construct validity remains contingent on whether the binary success metric maps to production correctness across vendors and operational contexts. External validity is limited: only one requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was used, tasks are synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies or routing convergence dynamics. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant pairs (3 of 1,199) limits power to detect small absolute effects; the bootstrap CI and discordant counts quantify that limitation.

Operational implications and next steps: Under conditions where initial generation commonly satisfies deterministic verifier checks, verifier‑assisted repair may be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a strict binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value more discriminatingly, future studies should (a) increase task ambiguity/adversariality, (b) vary verifier strictness, (c) test multiple LLM families and deployed vendor renderers, and (d) perform explicit per‑cluster (topology) confirmatory analyses when that hypothesis is intended as primary. The archived artifacts (see Methods pointers) enable exact reproduction and targeted sensitivity analyses.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench is a preregistered, artifact‑rich paired study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines. On the supplied synthetic/consented corpus and deterministic validator settings, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (~99.75%); the guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 pp (paired difference = 0.0025020851) but this change is not statistically significant (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Repair was invoked only three times and model_calls_used = 1,203. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a pooled‑separate confirmatory test; the archived confirmatory artifacts hold pooled inference only (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, execution/execution_manifest.json). The run’s artifacts, seeds, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code are archived to support reproducible follow‑ups that vary corpus difficulty, verifier strictness, and model families to identify conditions where verifier scaffolding yields operationally meaningful gains.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies, routing convergence, or transient telemetry seen in live networks.

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is documented in archived analysis artifacts.
Topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was preregistered but not executed as a pooled‑separate confirmatory test; only pooled confirmatory artifacts are archived.
